4lsa2m:121: The minimal unit should include: content, type, source, scope, confidence, timestamp, status. 555npd:278: Traditional RAG's retrieve(query) pattern relies on similarity, but for Agent Memory, the history that should influence the current task isn't necessarily semantically similar to the user's current question. This is a fundamental architectural difference. The solution — Progressive Disclosure (summary → memory index → rollout summary) — essentially layers "relevance judgment": first let the Agent know what's available, then decide whether to go deeper, rather than making the Agent face all memory fragments from the start. This approach has another benefit: when the Agent needs to know "roughly what I remember," it doesn't need to stuff all memories into the context.

9vbsrp:195: The article categorizes memory into three types: task, environment, and self. These three types have completely different update frequencies and reliability: task memory changes at any time, environment memory is relatively stable but has fuzzy boundaries, and self-memory is the most error-prone and hardest to verify. Mixing them in the same storage makes subsequent conflict detection, decay handling, and permission management extremely complex. Self-memory is especially special — it is the Agent's metacognition about its own past behavior, recording "what I inferred, which inferences were later falsified, and what types of tasks I'm good at." This type of memory inherently carries confidence annotations and requires periodic review.

m45bng:180: Understanding writes as "allocating future influence to history" is a precise metaphor. This means every write is not just a storage action, but also implies future retrieval cost, context cost, attention cost, and conflict management cost. The direct corollary of this thinking is: before writing, ask whether the memory, if frequently read in the future, would bring more benefit than the misinformation it might cause. This is especially true for Agent inference-type memories — they inherently carry an "unconfirmed" label, but once they enter context, the model tends to treat them as facts.
